client: I just... I don't know how to be okay anymore. Yesterday was my sister's favorite coffee shop's anniversary, and I couldn't even go inside without breaking down. I feel like I'm betraying her by trying to live my life, but I know she'd want me to be happy. It's all so messed up.
therapist: I hear how deeply painful this is for you—the grief feels so present, especially in those places that remind you of your sister. It sounds like there's a real struggle between knowing what she'd want for you and the guilt that comes with moving forward. What do you think your sister would say to you about that feeling of betrayal?

client: She'd probably tell me to stop being so hard on myself... she always said that when she was alive. But knowing that doesn't make the guilt go away. It's like my brain agrees with her, but my heart keeps punishing me for every moment I'm not completely shattered by her absence.
therapist: It sounds like there’s a real disconnect between what you logically know and what you emotionally feel—almost like your heart is holding onto the pain as a way to stay connected to her. What would it feel like to gently challenge that idea that being shattered is the only way to honor her?

client: It’s hard to even imagine challenging that idea... it feels like if I’m not in pain, I’m somehow forgetting her or letting her go. And I don’t want to let her go. But at the same time, I know this isn’t sustainable—I’m exhausted all the time, and I can barely focus on anything else. I just don’t know how to hold onto her memory without holding onto the hurt.
therapist: It sounds like you’re carrying such a heavy weight—wanting to honor her memory while also recognizing that the pain is draining you. It’s understandable to feel like letting go of the hurt might mean letting go of her, but what if holding onto her could look different? What’s one small way you could honor her memory that feels meaningful but not painful?

client: I guess I could do something she loved, like planting flowers or baking her favorite cookies. But even that feels complicated... like, what if I start crying halfway through? Or what if I can’t finish it because it’s too much? It’s hard to imagine doing anything without feeling overwhelmed.
therapist: It makes sense that these thoughts come up—anticipating the pain can sometimes feel as hard as the moment itself. What if we shifted the focus from "doing it perfectly" to simply allowing whatever emotions come up, even if that means tears? Could you try one small part of baking or planting, and just notice what happens without judging it?

client: I guess I could try baking just one batch of cookies instead of the whole recipe... but I’m worried it’ll just make me cry the whole time. And then I’ll feel like I failed at honoring her properly. It’s like I’m stuck between wanting to do something for her and being scared of how much it’ll hurt.
therapist: You're describing such an understandable tension—wanting to connect with her memory while bracing for the wave of grief. It sounds like there's a fear that tears might mean you're "failing" at honoring her, rather than being a natural part of the process. What would it feel like to consider that the tears might actually be part of honoring her, too?

client: That's... actually a really different way to think about it. I always saw crying as a sign of weakness, like I wasn't strong enough to handle missing her. But maybe the tears just show how much I still love her? It still feels scary though - like if I start crying, I might never stop.
therapist: That insight is so important—recognizing that tears can be an expression of love, not just pain. It makes sense that it still feels scary though; grief can sometimes make us afraid of being overwhelmed by emotions. What would it feel like to test that fear in a small way—maybe letting yourself cry for just a few minutes, then noticing what happens next?

client: I could try that... but part of me worries that if I let myself cry even a little, it'll all come rushing out and I won't be able to stop. Last time I really cried, I ended up staying in bed for two days. How do I know this time would be different? It feels like walking right up to the edge of a cliff.
therapist: It sounds like that fear of being overwhelmed by your emotions is holding you back—like letting yourself feel even a little might risk losing control. That’s such a understandable worry, especially after experiences where grief felt all-consuming. What if we approached it step by step—maybe setting a timer for a few minutes to cry, then checking in with yourself to see how you feel? Would that feel like a safer way to test the waters?

client: I could try the timer idea... but even the thought of setting it makes my chest feel tight. What if those few minutes make everything worse? Last time I tried to "control" my crying, it just made me feel more panicked, like I was fighting against myself. Maybe I'm not ready to face it head-on like that yet.
therapist: It sounds like even the idea of trying to manage your emotions brings up a lot of tension and fear—like trying to control it might make things feel harder, not easier. That’s completely valid, and it’s okay to take this at your own pace. What would it feel like to explore other ways to honor your sister that feel less overwhelming right now—maybe something gentle, like writing her a letter or looking at old photos?

client: Looking at photos might be... okay? I keep them all hidden in a box because seeing them hurts too much. But maybe just one photo, for a few seconds? I don't know why this feels so terrifying - it's just paper and ink, but it's like I'm scared the memories will swallow me whole. I think I could try it if I had someone with me, but I don't want to burden my friends with this.
therapist: It sounds like you’re carrying a lot of fear about facing those memories—like opening that box might unleash something overwhelming. That’s completely understandable, especially when grief feels so raw. What if you started with just one photo and kept it brief, almost like dipping your toe into the water? And if you’re worried about burdening friends, would it feel helpful to have a plan in place for how you’ll care for yourself afterward?

client: Maybe I could pick a happy photo, like from that beach trip we took. But what if looking at it makes me realize I'll never have new memories with her? That thought terrifies me more than anything. I like the idea of a self-care plan afterwards, but what if I just spiral and nothing helps?
therapist: It sounds like that fear of never making new memories with her is really holding you back—like looking at the photo might make the loss feel even more permanent. That’s such a deep and painful thought. What if, along with the self-care plan, you also prepared a gentle reminder for yourself—like a note saying, "This photo is a gift, not just a loss"? How does that feel?
